html:
In 1879 Tetteh Quarshie, a blacksmith from the Accra area, came home from the Spanish island of Fernando Po (now Bioko) with cocoa beans and planted a farm at Mampong in the Akuapem hills. Missionaries of the Basel Mission had tried growing cocoa earlier, but his farm is remembered as the true start of cocoa in the Gold Coast.

Farmers bought seed from him, and the crop spread fast. It needed little capital and suited the forest belt. Unlike plantation crops elsewhere, Gold Coast cocoa was grown mostly by African smallholders, who opened new land and built roads and towns with their profits. By about 1911 the colony was the world's largest producer.

Cocoa became the backbone of the economy of Ghana and paid for much of its early independence. Today neighbouring Ivory Coast grows even more. Tetteh Quarshie died in 1892.
